svg.aria-label: Diagram: the three ways a Google Cloud firewall rule picks its targets; why Google recommends service accounts over network tags for strict control because any principal who can edit an instance can change its tags and therefore which rules apply; the rule that service accounts and network tags cannot be mixed and which sources each target choice forbids; and the operational and scope trade-offs including live tag changes versus a required restart, the per-rule limits, and the fact that neither method reaches alias IP ranges or GKE Pods
svg.title: Targeting by network tag versus service account: three axes that point different ways
svg.text: Tags and service accounts are not two syntaxes for the same thing.
They differ on who can change them, whether you can change them live, and how many you get.
Three ways a rule picks its targets
OMIT THE TARGET — the rule applies to all instances in the VPC network. The default.
BY NETWORK TAG — applies if the instance has a tag matching at least one target tag.
BY SERVICE ACCOUNT — applies if the instance uses a matching target service account.
Targets identify the network INTERFACES of instances, including GKE nodes.
The security axis, where Google states a preference
If you need strict control over how firewall rules are applied to VMs, use target service
accounts and source service accounts instead of target and source network tags.
WHY: a network tag is an arbitrary attribute. Any IAM principal who can EDIT the instance
can change its tags — which could change the set of applicable firewall rules for it.
Compute Engine Instance Admin on the project is enough.
A service account is an IDENTITY. One per instance, and using it needs Service Account User.
You cannot mix them, and the target choice limits the sources
No rule may use target service accounts and target network tags together, ingress or egress.
Target NETWORK TAGS → source service accounts are invalid, and so is any combination of
source IP ranges with source service accounts.
Target SERVICE ACCOUNT → source network tags are invalid, and so is any combination of
source IP ranges with source network tags.
Operations and scope, where tags win and both fall short
LIVE CHANGE: tags can be added or removed while the instance is running. Changing a service
account requires stopping and restarting the instance.
SCALE: 70 target tags per rule against 10 target service accounts; 30 source tags against 10.
SCOPE, the one to remember: a tag-based rule applies to the instance’s PRIMARY INTERNAL IP.
And service account rules apply to the GKE NODE, not the GKE Pod.
So neither method reaches an alias IP range cleanly — #64 again, for a third time.
Writing rules needs compute.firewalls.create and Compute Security Admin; reading them needs
only Compute Network Viewer — so who may see the policy and who may change it are separate.
The choice is not style. Tags are editable by whoever can edit the VM, which makes the rule
set only as strong as instance-edit permissions. Service accounts move that into IAM.
